article_title: Achievement and Growth Norms for Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills
citation: Wei He, NWEA Psychometrics and Analytics. (2026). Achievement and Growth Norms for Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/spanish-map-reading-fluency-technical-report/
title: Use normative results alongside other evidence of student learning, not as the sole basis for placement or instructional decisions
description: The report cautions that although the achievement and growth norms provide context for interpreting student performance at a point in time and growth over time, "decisions about student placement or instructional planning should not rely on norms alone." Educators are advised to consider normative results together with other evidence such as classroom performance and teacher observations, because test scores alone have limited meaning without appropriate context.
requirements: Educators must supplement norm-referenced scores with other evidence of student learning, such as classroom performance and teacher observations
constraints: The norms reflect a norming sample concentrated in the South (particularly Texas) and in early grades, which the report says provides important context for interpretation
target_learners: Students in grades K-3 assessed with Spanish MAP Reading Fluency
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of student achievement and growth in foundational Spanish reading skills
examples: The report's conclusion states the norms offer context for schools, educators, and parents to understand performance relative to peers in the norming sample, supporting more informed evaluation of student outcomes.

article_title: Foundations of Collaboration
citation: Thevenard, P., Shell, A., Victor, L., Glazer, K., Fusco, J., Tyler, C., and Akanbi, K. (2025, May). Foundations of Collaboration. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/253
title: Establish norms and belonging-supporting processes before and during group work; simply putting students in groups can be ineffective or harmful
description: The primer recommends that teachers be intentional about fostering relationships, designing equitable learning experiences, and challenging exclusionary practices during group work. It warns that "Simply putting students in groups without establishing norms and processes that reinforce a sense of belonging can be ineffective and potentially harmful." Teachers cannot control institutional dynamics but can cultivate a classroom culture that nurtures and prioritizes belonging.
requirements: Deliberate steps to provide learners with concrete collaborative skills, including explicitly teaching collaborative skills, facilitating respectful dialogue, and addressing instances of exclusion
constraints: Teachers cannot control the many and shifting dynamics of their institution; classroom culture is the part they can cultivate
target_learning_goals: Effective collaboration
Inclusive participation
Belonging
examples: The primer's strategies table pairs characteristics of collaborative learning (grouping, positive interdependence, accountability, interpersonal skills, reflection) with concrete belonging-fostering activities.

article_title: Encouraging Social and Emotional Learning in the Context of New Accountability
citation: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability
title: Do not use measures of students' social-emotional competencies for high-stakes accountability
description: The report concludes that "States should not use measures of students' social and emotional competence for high-stakes accountability purposes, at least for now." Most such surveys are relatively new, were not designed for cross-school comparison, and are vulnerable to reference bias because students are not always the best judges of their own competence. States can instead support local use of these measures to inform teaching, learning, and program investments, with aggregate reporting for school decisions.
requirements: If used at all, measures should be used locally to identify students' strengths and needs, reported on an aggregate basis to inform school decisions
constraints: Measures may be particularly vulnerable to reference bias; attaching consequences may lead individuals to fake or game a measure, rendering it invalid
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of social-emotional competencies for improvement rather than sanction
examples: The report recommends student surveys of their own social-emotional competencies for state-supported and locally selected tiers, not the federal tier

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: North Coast Teacher Residency Consortium: a half-time special education residency that lets paraeducators keep their salaries while training
description: The Humboldt County Office of Education and Humboldt State University launched this residency in fall 2019 to recruit existing special education paraeducators across 32 primarily rural districts. "Paraeducator residents keep their jobs during the residency but are guaranteed to spend at least 50% of every day in a class setting working with a special education mentor teacher." Residents earn salaries of $18,127 to $25,635 plus benefits, receive $10,000 tuition and testing-fee coverage, and attend evening courses, with remotely located residents using distance learning tools.
requirements: Partnership agreements guaranteeing the 50% clinical fieldwork minimum and release time for program requirements, including site-swap systems; a $9,000 supplemental site budget for mentor stipends and substitutes
constraints: The program was in its first year, so results were too early to show; half-time placements are a compromise, as full-time paid placements would be ideal
target_learners: Employed special education paraeducators seeking certification
target_learning_goals: Full special education credential preparation
Co-planning, curriculum design, and whole-class and small-group teaching with mentor support
examples: Eight of the 10 inaugural residents were paraeducators; by year's end, 9 of 10 residents had full-time teaching positions, and the program reported strong demand for the next cohort.

article_title: It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
citation: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction.
title: Make prediction, evaluation, and reflection non-delegable components of every AI-integrated task
description: The principle holds that when AI is integrated into instruction, the epistemic operations of predicting outcomes before AI engagement, evaluating AI outputs against expectations, and reflecting on the division of cognitive work must remain with the learner. The authors state that "AIRIS prevents this by making prediction, evaluation, and reflection non-delegable components of every task", countering a cumulative hollowing-out of epistemic engagement from incremental AI accommodations.
requirements: Tasks must be designed so students generate their own expectations before AI is introduced
Teachers must monitor whether students critically compare AI outputs against their own predictions or simply accept them
constraints: Addresses risk at the level of individual instructional design, not at the level of the education system
target_learning_goals: preserving epistemic engagement and scientific reasoning practices under AI augmentation
examples: In the Inquire phase of the elevator task, students estimate maximum speed without AI and compare AI-generated diagrams with their own Phase 1 sketches, annotating discrepancies
key_sources: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13812

article_title: To Tab or Not to Tab: Measuring Critical Engagement in AI Code Completion Tools Using Behavioral Signals and Attention Checks
citation: Jessica Hutchison, Ian Tyler Applebaum, Kenneth Angelikas, Kush Rakesh Patel, Phuoc Nguyen, Antonio Lazaro, Nicholas Rucinski, Rahad Arman Nabid, and Stephen MacNeil. (2026). To Tab or Not to Tab: Measuring Critical Engagement in AI Code Completion Tools Using Behavioral Signals and Attention Checks. Proceedings of the 31st ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3803400.3809394
title: No single behavioral metric reliably captures critical engagement with AI code suggestions
description: The article concludes that because interaction metrics were weakly or inconsistently correlated with task performance, while some behaviors such as tab acceptance were strongly associated with failed attention checks, educators and researchers should interpret behavioral metrics as a pattern rather than rely on any one measure. The authors state that "no single metric reliably captures critical engagement" and that metrics may reflect a complex mix of reflective reasoning, over-reliance, or negative expertise.
requirements: Multiple behavioral metrics should be logged and interpreted together, including acceptance behaviors, dwell time, execution frequency, and attention check performance
constraints: Dwell time is ambiguous: it may indicate deliberate reasoning, superficial engagement, or negative expertise where experienced students quickly reject low-quality suggestions
Findings come from a single problem, single model, and a single class at one university
target_learners: Novice programmers using AI code completion tools
target_learning_goals: Assessing critical engagement with AI-generated code
examples: In the 55-student study, number of runs correlated positively with task performance yet also positively with failed attention checks, showing productive behaviors can coexist with lapses in critical engagement

article_title: Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models
citation: Naiming Liu, Xinghe Chen, Richard Baraniuk, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Shashank Sonkar. (2026). Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00818
title: Two complementary misconception-acquisition formalizations: the Novice Student Misconception Model and the Expert Tutor Misconception Model
description: The article formalizes misconception acquisition from two perspectives. The Novice Student Misconception Model simulates an individual student holding one specific misconception and must satisfy Misconception Replication on applicable types plus Correct Reasoning Preservation on non-applicable types. The Expert Tutor Misconception Model captures the spectrum of misconceptions a tutor encounters across students, a computational analogue of teachers' Knowledge of Student Misconceptions, and must replicate every training misconception while maintaining Overall Correct Accuracy across all problem types. Both use thresholds where "We setθm =θ c = 90%in all experiments."
requirements: Acquisition is defined by printed thresholds: MA at or above the misconception threshold on applicable types and correct accuracy at or above the correctness threshold on the required problem-type set.
constraints: The tutor model must solve all problem types correctly when prompted, not just non-applicable ones, making its criterion more demanding than the student model's.
target_learners: Individual algebra students (student model) and tutors recognizing error patterns across a student population (tutor model)
target_learning_goals: Faithful simulation of misconception-driven errors and recognition of diverse student error patterns
examples: Experiments instantiated both models by fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Phi-4-4B-Mini, and Qwen-3-4B-Instruct, each first trained on 2000 correct examples per problem type to reach OCA of at least 90%.
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Xinghe Chen, Richard Baraniuk, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Shashank Sonkar. (2026). Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00818

article_title: The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations
citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: Non-compensatory capped-bucket grading across topic-by-tier matrix cells
description: The grading architecture rejects compensatory scoring in favor of "Non-Compensatory Grading": instructors configure capped buckets per topic and cognitive tier, and the total score aggregates min(cap, earned points) per cell. Points per interaction follow P(b,s,k) = γk·V(b,s), where V(b,s) is monotonically increasing with the Bloom level and γk discounts assisted performance. Once a bucket is full, further low-level answers yield zero additional points, preventing grinding of foundational questions from compensating for missing higher-order evidence.
requirements: Instructor-defined 2D grading matrix (or 1D topic-level caps in Organic Mode) with point capacities per tier and deterministic logging of Bloom level and hint count per interaction
constraints: Students cannot manually pivot between cognitive tiers within a topic, as foundational tiers must be completed to scaffold advanced topics
target_learners: higher education students in instructor-configured courses
target_learning_goals: demonstrating mastery at each required cognitive tier rather than accumulating low-level points
examples: Table 2 shows a conceptual matrix for an introductory Economics course with tier caps of 10-15 points and a 100-point total; Appendix A walks through a 40-point Price Controls topic at 120% oversampling
key_sources: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624

article_title: Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency
citation: Sverrir Thorgeirsson, Theo B. Weidmann, and Zhendong Su. 2026. Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791666
title: Purpose-built no-code vibe-coding research platform for controlled experimentation
description: A custom web platform built for controlled study of LLM-native software creation. Unlike commercial tools, "our own platform deliberately conceals the code entirely, consistent with the original definition of vibe coding", retaining a chat window on the left and app preview on the right, with rollback, a blurred live stream of model output, task descriptions, and a timer. It was informed by a survey of Replit, Cursor, Lovable, and Bolt, runs on Claude Sonnet 4 with a diff-based update mechanism, and logs feature exploration of sample applications to support reproducible, privacy-compliant evaluation.
requirements: The integrated AI model must not retain participant inputs or train on participants' prompts, per the ethics committee's data-protection requirements.
constraints: Exposing source code is intentionally avoided, as it would introduce an additional interaction mode and risk confounding the pure vibe-coding construct.
target_learners: tertiary-level students in controlled laboratory studies
target_learning_goals: measuring proficiency in iterative, behavior-guided natural-language programming
examples: The authors built the sample applications with the platform itself and instrumented them to track and display whether participants had tried all features before submission.

title: Noun-ending form-focused instruction embedded in subject-matter teaching

The treatment targets written and oral gender-attribution accuracy in immersion students.

Selected noun endings that reliably predict grammatical gender
Opportunities for practice in associating endings with gender attribution

examples: Three teachers each taught two classes with the FFI treatment while a fourth teacher taught the same subject matter without FFI to two comparison classes

article_title: The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying
citation: Peadar Donohoe and Carmel O’Sullivan. (2015). The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying. Scenario, Volume 2015 · Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.33178/scenario.9.1.6
title: No name, no blame discussion of bullying incidents
description: The BPP adopts the 'no name, no blame' approach (Maines and Robinson 1997) when learners discuss real bullying incidents: peers describe what happened and the player roles involved without identifying or blaming any child. Teachers in both strands and all learner focus groups reported this approach was a significant aid to the discussions, as one fourth-class participant put it: "we could just tell out what happened without feeling bad about it". It enables honest peer discussion of feelings and incidents within the metacognitive peer-learning environment.
requirements: Discussion facilitation by the teacher with the no-name, no-blame norm established
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive discussion of bullying incidents and feelings
Empathy for those targeted
examples: Learners voluntarily described school incidents and named the Bullying Circle player types involved without naming or blaming any peer

article_title: Neural correlates of theory of mind reasoning in congenitally blind children
citation: Richardson H., Saxe R., Bedny M. (2023). Neural correlates of theory of mind reasoning in congenitally blind children. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2023.101285
title: Non-visual story-based behavioral ToM task for blind and sighted children
description: A validated, non-visual story-based task measuring ToM reasoning in children aged four to twelve, publicly available at https://osf.io/pavdg/. Children listen to an experimenter read twenty short stories and answer 51 questions, including 22 two-alternative forced choice and 29 open-ended explanation questions targeting "desires, expectations, beliefs, intentions, perceptual access, and knowledge of the characters." Items vary the source modality of mental states (visual, aural, amodal) to test whether blind children show differential comprehension of visual experiences, and 19 control questions verify attention and comprehension.
requirements: Requires children to be fluent English speakers, as stories are read aloud in English and answered verbally
constraints: Designed for use with four- to twelve-year-old children
target_learners: children aged 4-12, including congenitally blind children
target_learning_goals: theory of mind reasoning about beliefs, desires, emotions, and perceptual access
examples: Validated against a previously used ToM task in 21 sighted children: the two tasks correlated even controlling for age and verbal and non-verbal IQ (b=0.46, t=2.6, p=.02)
key_sources: Richardson H., Saxe R., Bedny M. (2023). Neural correlates of theory of mind reasoning in congenitally blind children. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2023.101285

article_title: Learning styles concepts and evidence
citation: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2009). Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Volume 9 Number 3. https://journals.sagepub.com/
title: Do not adopt learning-styles assessments in general educational practice; devote resources to practices with strong evidence bases
description: The review recommends that, given the absence of adequate evidence for learning-styles-based instruction, educators should not incorporate learning-styles assessments into general practice. It states that "limited education resources would better be devoted to adopting other educational practices that have a strong evidence base, of which there are an increasing number." Any further research on learning-styles assessment should use designs capable of detecting the required crossover interaction.
requirements: Any future validation research must classify learners by style, randomly assign methods within style groups, use a common outcome test, and test for a style-by-method crossover interaction
constraints: The review does not claim all versions of learning styles have been refuted; many remain untested, so this is a recommendation against current adoption, not a conclusive refutation
target_learners: Students at all educational levels, kindergarten through graduate school
target_learning_goals: Allocating instructional resources to evidence-based practices rather than style-matched instruction
examples: The review's search found at most one arguable positive study and several methodologically strong studies with negative results, leading to the conclusion that classroom application of learning styles is unwarranted at present
key_sources: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2009). Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Volume 9 Number 3. https://journals.sagepub.com/

article_title: Writing fluency and quality in kindergarten and first grade: the role of attention, reading, transcription, and oral language
citation: Kent, S., Wanzek, J., Petscher, Y., Al Otaiba, S. S., & Kim, Y.-S. (2014). Writing fluency and quality in kindergarten and first grade: The role of attention, reading, transcription, and oral language. Reading and Writing, 27(7), 1163-1188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-013-9480-1
title: Not-So-Simple View of Writing with attention as a component factor in early writing development
description: Berninger and Winn's Not-So-Simple View of Writing proposes three primary components: transcription; executive functions regulating focused attention, inhibitory control, and mental shifting during planning, reviewing, and revising; and text generation, the transformation of ideas to language representations. This study's SEM results, in the authors' words, "lend support to their theory at the stage of beginning writing," because a model including attention fit better and attention uniquely predicted fluency and quality concurrently and longitudinally.
requirements: Assessment of attention/self-regulation alongside literacy, transcription, and oral language component skills
constraints: The study assessed only teacher ratings of attention; executive functions such as working memory and self-regulation strategies were not assessed, so support at this age covers supervisory attention only
target_learning_goals: Writing fluency and writing quality (compositional production, ideation, organization, word choice)
examples: A SEM of 265 kindergarten and first-grade students in which the attention factor was included alongside literacy, letter-writing fluency, and oral language factors predicting compositional fluency and quality

article_title: How do different aspects of spatial skills relate to early arithmetic and number line estimation?
citation: Véronique Cornu, Caroline Hornung, Christine Schiltz, Romain Martin. (2017). The predictive role of spatial skills for arithmetic and number line estimation in kindergarten children. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2017.09.002
title: Spatial skills are non-unitary: orientation, visualization and visuo-motor integration are distinct aspects relevant to early mathematics
description: The article treats spatial skills as a non-unitary construct whose different aspects must be differentiated when studying numerical development. It operationalizes three aspects — a spatial orientation task, a spatial visualization task and a visuo-motor integration task — administered at kindergarten to predict later arithmetic and number line estimation. The abstract notes that "due to the construct’s non-unitary nature, different aspects of spatial skills need to be differentiated". This differentiation framework organizes the study's predictor set and motivates its finding that spatial orientation is the key spatial predictor.
requirements: Spatial skills must be measured with separate tasks capturing distinct aspects (orientation, visualization, visuo-motor integration) rather than a single composite
constraints: The framework was examined in kindergarten children predicting arithmetic and number line estimation within a four-month window
target_learning_goals: early arithmetic
number line estimation
understanding numerical development
examples: The study administered a spatial orientation task, a spatial visualization task and a visuo-motor integration task at Time 1 to 125 kindergarten children
key_sources: Véronique Cornu, Caroline Hornung, Christine Schiltz, Romain Martin. (2017). The predictive role of spatial skills for arithmetic and number line estimation in kindergarten children. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2017.09.002

article_title: Learning-by-Teaching Without Audience Presence or Interaction: When and Why Does it Work?
citation: Lachner, A., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Renkl, A. (2022). Learning-by-Teaching Without Audience Presence or Interaction: When and Why Does it Work? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09643-4
title: Three proposed mechanism views of learning by non-interactive teaching: retrieval practice, generative processing, and social presence
description: The review organizes its account of why non-interactive teaching works around three not mutually exclusive explanatory views. The retrieval practice view treats explaining as a special case of retrieval; the generative processing view holds that explaining additionally triggers inference-making, organization, and elaboration; and the social presence view argues that the actual, implied, or imagined audience shapes the extent of generative processing. As the review states: "There are three (not mutually exclusive) main views that aim to explain the beneficial effects of learning by non-interactive teaching: (1) retrieval practice, (2) generative processing, and (3) social presence (of an actual/implied/imagined audience)." The social presence view is further decomposed into discourse pragmatics, affective (arousal), and motivational perspectives.
requirements: Empirical studies that experimentally compare non-interactive teaching with retrieval, self-explaining, or restudy conditions to test the mechanisms
constraints: The review notes most research did not explicitly or systematically test these different assumptions, so the evidence for each view is preliminary
target_learning_goals: Deep comprehension and transfer of studied content through explaining it to an audience
key_sources: Lachner, A., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Renkl, A. (2022). Learning-by-Teaching Without Audience Presence or Interaction: When and Why Does it Work? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09643-4

article_title: The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education
citation: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y
title: Do not assume a universal ideal number of external representations; tailor representational sets to learners and context
description: The article explicitly cautions against seeking one optimal number of representations: "it is not reasonable to assume that there is a universal, ideal number of representations for learning and problem-solving in STEM." Because personal and environmental factors vary significantly across individuals and contexts, the meaningful number of representations may vary across contexts and disciplines. Design decisions about how many representations to use should therefore be conditioned on moderators the review identifies, above all the provision of appropriate instructional support, rather than on a fixed rule.
requirements: Design decisions should account for moderating factors such as educational level, instructional support, informational redundancy, mode of presentation, and representational homogeneity.
constraints: The possible influences of including more than two external representations in STEM learning remain unknown in several respects, and future research on representation novelty is needed.
target_learners: Students of any age in STEM education
target_learning_goals: Effective design of multirepresentational learning materials
examples: The review examined educational level, support, mode of presentation, redundancy, and homogeneity as moderators rather than prescribing a fixed number of representations.
key_sources: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y

article_title: A red button does it all: A red button nudges students to close their knowledge gaps in an intelligent tutoring system
citation: Spitzer, M. W. H., Moeller, K., Richter, E., Frede, L., & Bardach, L. (2025). A red button does it all: A red button nudges students to close their knowledge gaps in an intelligent tutoring system. Learning and Instruction 99 (2025) 102181. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102181
title: Incorporate notification badges as low-effort nudges to prompt students to engage with adaptively provided learning materials
description: Because adaptively provided additional learning materials sit in a separate tab that students may never open, ITSs can add notification badges (e.g., a small red button showing the number of open gaps) as automatic, low-effort nudges. The article argues badges "direct attention without requiring active thought" and so likely reduce extraneous cognitive load, consistent with Cognitive Load Theory, and draws on color-in-context theory for red's attention-drawing urgency. The study's natural experiment supports the badge's effectiveness at raising gap closing.
requirements: The badge must signal system-identified knowledge gaps and update (be removed or reduced) as gaps are closed.
constraints: Offering materials directly may disrupt lesson plans when all students are expected to work on the same teacher-assigned tasks; the badge approach relies on students still choosing to engage with the materials.
target_learners: Students in grades 4 to 12 learning mathematics using an ITS
target_learning_goals: Engaging with adaptively assigned additional learning materials to close knowledge gaps
examples: In bettermarks, a red notification badge on the knowledge gaps tab displayed a white digit reflecting the number of additional learning materials a student should complete.

article_title: Learning by writing: The influence of handwriting and typing on novel word learning in typically developing readers and readers with dyslexia
citation: Cerni, Tania; Lonciari, Isabella; Job, Remo. (2025). Learning by writing: The influence of handwriting and typing on novel word learning in typically developing readers and readers with dyslexia. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102119
title: Nonword learning paradigm comparing typing and handwriting with spelling and nonword-image association tests
description: The study used a paradigm in which participants learned nonwords varying in transcription regularity, each paired with an image, through either typing or handwriting. Learning was tested with spelling and nonword-image association tasks. The article states that "Recorded metrics included accuracy, writing duration during learning and spelling tasks, and reaction time in the nonword-image mapping task." Eighteen Italian middle school students with developmental dyslexia and eighteen age-matched typically developing readers participated.
requirements: Nonwords must vary in transcription regularity and be paired with images
Both a spelling task and a nonword-image mapping task are needed to assess orthographic and semantic learning
constraints: Evaluated with Italian middle school students, so findings are scoped to that language and age group
target_learning_goals: orthographic learning
semantic word-referent association
examples: Participants learned a set of nonwords, varying in transcription regularity, paired with images, either through typing or handwriting

article_title: Variability in memory span.
citation: Mitchell, David. (1918). Variability in Memory Span. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Variability+in+Memory+Span%22+Mitchell+1918
title: Do not grade a child's ability from a single examination, since performance varies from day to day
description: The article argues that educational and intelligence grading has assumed individual performance is constant, and that its memory span results show "The performance ability of children is not a static or fixed quantity." Because a child may score very differently on the same task on different days, a single examination can misrank him. The author recommends that "the doubt should always be in favor of the child until a wider range of experiment with him has been possible."
requirements: Multiple testing occasions are needed before a single low score is treated as evidence of a child's inability.
constraints: The author notes the results are not conclusive evidence that mental testing rests on a false assumption, and that variability under intelligence-scale procedures still needs to be determined.
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of individual ability and intelligence
examples: The study tested 192 fifth graders on two days five weeks apart and 97 seventh graders on ten successive school days, finding individual scores varying by as much as six within a range of ten.

article_title: The correlation of general intelligence tests and school standing.
citation: E. B. Skaggs. (1918). The Correlation of General Intelligence Tests and School Standing. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Never brand a child as feeble-minded on the bare intelligence rating alone; consider heredity, training, environment, disease history, and sense-organ conditions
description: A diagnostic-caution principle: an intelligence rating should never by itself determine a label of feeble-mindedness. The article states that "No one would think of branding a child as feeble-minded until many other factors besides the bare intelligence rating had been taken into consideration, as heredity, training, environment, disease history, sense-organ conditions, etc." It follows from the author's argument that tests tap only part of the child.
requirements: Multiple factors beyond the bare intelligence rating must be taken into consideration before any diagnostic label is applied.
constraints: The article frames this for diagnostic and prognostic use of mental tests, which it says have many weak points.
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis and prognosis of student ability
examples: The author reports illustrations of each stated limitation from limited use of prominent mental tests over the last four years.

article_title: A combined mental-educational survey.
citation: Pintner, R., and Marshall, H. (1920). A Combined Mental-Educational Survey. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Combined+Mental-Educational+Survey+Pintner+Marshall
title: Non-Language Mental Test: a group intelligence test usable from grade II upwards and fair to non-English-speaking and deaf children
description: The Non-Language Mental Test is a group intelligence test devised to have as wide an application as possible and to be far removed from ordinary school work, by avoiding reading and language demands. The article states it is useful for school children from grade II upwards and "can be given with equal fairness to English-speaking as well as to non-English speaking or deaf children". It supplies the mental index against which educational attainment is compared, and reduces overrating of bookish children.
requirements: Standardization on children who have taken both tests, so that ability and attainment indices are mutually comparable
constraints: The authors note it does not overlap at all with school-taught content, making it a gauge of native ability rather than achievement; its Binet agreement coefficients were obtained only for grades 3 to 6
target_learners: school children from grade II upwards
target_learning_goals: measuring native mental ability independent of schooling and language
examples: Used with the Educational Survey Test on 4303 children to derive the index and Difference tables

article_title: Instructional compensation for age-related cognitive declines: Effects of goal specificity in maze learning.
citation: Paas, F., Camp, G., & Rikers, R.M.J.P. (2001). Instructional compensation for age-related cognitive declines: Effects of goal specificity in maze learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 93(1), 181-186. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.93.1.181
title: Use nonspecific rather than specific goals when instructing older learners on complex tasks
description: The article shows that presenting a task's finish point "in more general terms" rather than as a specific location reduced the performance disadvantage of old adults in maze learning. Because a specific goal disproportionately compromised elderly performance while its absence disproportionately enhanced it, designers of instruction for older learners should favor nonspecific goal formulations. The recommendation rests on the authors' conclusion that cognitive load theory-based instruction can compensate for age-related cognitive declines.
requirements: Instruction must involve a task, such as maze navigation, whose goal can be formulated either specifically or in general terms.
constraints: Evidence comes from a single computerized maze-learning study with 40 young and 40 old adults; the article does not claim generalization beyond such tasks.
target_learning_goals: complex task performance such as maze navigation
examples: In the experiment, the maze finish point was presented either as a specific location or in more general terms, and the age difference was much smaller in the nonspecific goal conditions.

article_title: Distribution of grades.
citation: J. L. Zerbe. (1917). Distribution of Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VIII(10), 575-588.
title: Normal-curve-based uniform grading standard (George Washington University committee plan)
description: A grading framework grounded in the psychological finding that mental ability, "when sufficiently large numbers are considered," is distributed in the bell-shaped probability curve. The George Washington University committee translated this into fixed grade percentages: "The grade of A or excellent should be assigned to about 4 per cent, of the students, B or good to about 24 per cent., C or medium to about 44 per cent., D or sub-medium to about 24 per cent, and E or failure to about 4 per cent." The article presents this plan, adopted since the University of Missouri's 1908 system, as the leading institutional attempt to replace personal-opinion grading with a uniform standard, while insisting it does not curtail teachers' freedom.
requirements: Faculty-wide adoption so that all teachers use approximately the same standard with all students, preserving uniformity across courses and instructors.
constraints: The committee itself allowed that failure percentages may properly be higher in lower classes and in professional schools, so the fixed percentages are adjustable rather than absolute.
target_learning_goals: fair and uniform evaluation of student achievement for credits, honors, and recommendations
examples: The George Washington University committee report of March 1914, quoted in the article, and the University of Missouri's 1908 adoption of a defined grading method.
key_sources: J. L. Zerbe. (1917). Distribution of Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VIII(10), 575-588. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074694

article_title: The effect of practice upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension.
citation: Whipple, G. M. (1910). The effect of practise upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=Whipple+effect+of+practise+range+of+visual+attention+apprehension
title: Do not expect brief daily perception exercises to train a general capacity to attend
description: The article argues against classroom exercises, like Miss Aiken's, that claim to train concentration of attention through brief daily drills. Its experiments show practise effects on quick visual perception are negligible once habituation and grouping devices are removed, and individual differences are material-specific. It concludes these considerations "make it still more improbable that a series of classroom exercises, like Miss Aiken's, will train and develop general capacity to attend."
requirements: Any claim of attention training must be tested against material other than that used in the training exercises
constraints: The article concedes the negative outcome is not entirely conclusive: practise may not have been sufficiently long, and observers were adults rather than children
target_learners: school pupils and adult learners targeted by mind-training exercises
target_learning_goals: concentration of attention and quick visual perception
examples: Whipple replicated Aiken-style exercises under laboratory conditions with college students and adults and measured the extent and nature of the improvement

article_title: Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality.
citation: Limpo, T., & Alves, R. A. (2013). Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105, 401-413. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031391
title: Not-so-simple view of writing with a capacity account of transcription–self-regulation development
description: The article organizes writing development around the not-so-simple view of writing (Berninger & Winn, 2006), in which "text generation is supported by the collaboration between transcription (handwriting and spelling) and high-level cognitive skills for self-regulation, such as planning and revising." Within working-memory constraints, transcription and self-regulation compete for attentional resources; as transcription automatizes across schooling, spare resources support planning and revising, shifting writers from knowledge telling toward knowledge transforming. The study's SEM results are offered as support for this account.
requirements: Assessment separating transcription skill from text-quality scoring, since poor spelling and penmanship bias holistic quality judgments
constraints: The account is tested only at Grades 4-6 and 7-9 with the specific indicators used; working memory and writing knowledge were not included in the model
target_learning_goals: Written composition quality in narrative and opinion genres
examples: Multiple-group SEM across Grades 4-6 and 7-9 with 376 students tested the model's developmental shift from direct to indirect transcription effects
key_sources: Limpo, T., & Alves, R. A. (2013). Modeling writing development: Contribution of transcription and self-regulation to Portuguese students' text generation quality. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105, 401-413. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031391

article_title: The dimensions of reading comprehension in Dutch children: Is differentiation by text and question type necessary?
citation: M.M.L. Muijselaar, N.M. Swart, E.G. Steenbeek-Planting, M. Droop, L. Verhoeven, P.F. de Jong. (2017). The dimensions of reading comprehension in Dutch children: Is differentiation by text and question type necessary? Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(1), 70-83. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000120
title: Do not assume separate comprehension abilities by text or question type when assessing fourth-grade reading comprehension
description: Because specific measures of comprehension differing by text and question type showed little systematic variation beyond a general factor, assessments of fourth-grade reading comprehension need not be differentiated by text or question type to capture distinct underlying abilities. The article's question — "Is differentiation by text and question type necessary?" — is answered negatively in its data: items largely reflect a common factor.
requirements: Applies to summarizing overall reading comprehension ability rather than diagnosing item-format-specific skills
constraints: Based on Dutch fourth-grade children and the text and question types studied
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension assessment and interpretation
examples: Multitrait, multimethod modeling of a text-by-question-type item pool administered to 996 children

article_title: Nonlinear relations between achievement and academic self-concepts in elementary and secondary school: An integrative data analysis across 13 countries.
citation: Keller, L., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2020). Nonlinear Relations Between Achievement and Academic Self-Concepts in Elementary and Secondary School: An Integrative Data Analysis Across 13 Countries. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000533
title: Do not assume a general linear trend when assessing and interpreting students' academic self-concepts
description: Because relations between achievement and self-concepts are nonlinear for a substantial share of students, practitioners "should be aware that there is no general linear trend between students' achievement and their corresponding academic self-concepts" and should account for this "when assessing and interpreting students' academic self-concepts in counseling contexts". Researchers are similarly advised to specify nonlinear models, including for elementary students, to avoid missing nonlinear relations.
requirements: Access to achievement and self-concept measures spanning the achievement continuum, ideally representative samples without range restriction
constraints: Nonlinear effects in elementary students were heterogeneous across countries and methods, and the study could not distinguish developmental causes from differences in the constructs assessed (reading vs. verbal self-concept)
target_learning_goals: valid assessment and interpretation of academic self-concepts in counseling
examples: The integrative data analysis applied quadratic and interrupted regression analyses to TIMSS, PIRLS, and PISA data as nonlinear alternatives to linear regression models

article_title: Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication
citation: Koch, S. B. J., Tyborowska, A., Niermann, H. C. M., Cillessen, A. H. N., Roelofs, K., Bašnáková, J., Toni, I., & Stolk, A. (2024). Integrating stereotypes and factual evidence in interpersonal communication. npj Science of Learning 9, 52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00262-6
title: Nonverbal communication game quantifying stereotype- and interaction-driven adjustments
description: A two-player digital game board with a 3 × 3 grid on which participants guide a partner (a role-blind confederate) to a hidden acorn by moving a bird avatar. Only the participant knows the location and only the partner can collect the object, driving dyads to "achieve mutual understanding by aligning on a limited but idiosyncratic number of strategies." Dyads solved trials well above chance (89.8 ± 11.7% against a chance level of 7.7%), indicating participants generated communicative behaviors that, despite their novelty, could be mutually understood. The game measures stereotype-driven adjustment (time spent in the object square) and interaction-driven convergence across eight blocks with alternating presumed partners.
requirements: A role-blind confederate performing both presumed-partner roles so that adjustments reflect stereotype beliefs rather than partner behavior
constraints: Minimizes linguistic conventions, so findings may not generalize to verbal communication with its prosodic and lexical cues
target_learners: adolescent participants in dyadic social interaction studies
target_learning_goals: measuring real-time communicative adjustment to partner beliefs and interaction dynamics
examples: Participants alternated between presumed child and adult partners over eight blocks of five trials, with the confederate blind to which role he performed.

article_title: Early reading at first grade predicts adult reading at age 42 in typical and dyslexic readers
citation: Emilio Ferrer, Bennett A. Shaywitz, John M. Holahan and Sally E. Shaywitz. (2023). Early reading at first grade predicts adult reading at age 42 in typical and dyslexic readers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00205-7
title: Do not require periodic retesting of adults with childhood-identified dyslexia seeking accommodations
description: The article argues that standardized testing agencies requiring applicants requesting accommodations to be retested every three or five years is not supported by longitudinal evidence. Because early reading level and the grade 1-5 trajectory strongly predict adult reading, "once a person is identified as dyslexic in the early grades, he or she is very likely to be dyslexic as an adult at age 42." This principle applies to accommodation policy for adult dyslexic readers.
requirements: Dyslexia identification must have occurred in the early grades with documented reading assessment
constraints: Findings come from one epidemiologic US cohort of primary English speakers followed to age 42
target_learning_goals: reading proficiency
access to accommodations for reading tasks
examples: The longitudinal data show dyslexic readers identified via WJ Reading Cluster and WISC-R criteria in grades 2 or 4 still showed substantial adult reading differences at age 42 on all ART-2 measures.

article_title: ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring
citation: Ghergulescu, I. & Muntean, C. H. (2016). ToTCompute: A Novel EEG-Based TimeOnTask Threshold Computation Mechanism for Engagement Modelling and Monitoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0111-2
title: Non-disturbing engagement monitoring via game-play interaction logging and physiological sensing
description: The article distinguishes disturbing methods (questionnaires interrupting game-play) from non-disturbing methods that monitor engagement "without interrupting the game-play and game flow". Non-disturbing methods log player behaviour automatically and may add physiological equipment such as EEG or eye-tracking. ToTCompute exemplifies this pattern by combining game-playing event logs (task start/stop timestamps) with continuous EEG-based engagement recording during game-play.
requirements: Automatic logging embedded in the game to record task start and stop timestamps
Clear, independent game tasks for which metrics can be computed
constraints: Additional equipment such as EEG adds cost and is harder to incorporate in everyday game-based e-learning scenarios
target_learning_goals: continuous engagement monitoring during learning games
examples: The Fire Protocol case study embedded automatic logging in the game and recorded EEG with the Emotiv EPOC headset while participants played.

article_title: Unlocking the Everdoor: analyzing the serious game Spiritfarer
citation: Noah Glaser, Lucas Jensen, Tina Riedy, Maggie Center, Jim Shifflett, Joseph Griffin. (2024). Unlocking the Everdoor: analyzing the serious game Spiritfarer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10357-x
title: Design serious games about difficult topics with cozy, low-stress mechanics and no fail states so emotional engagement is sustained without frustration
description: The article's design recommendation, drawn from participant responses and discussion, is that games addressing heavy themes benefit from comforting, forgiving mechanics. The article reports that "There was no fail state or possibility of losing, and even mistakes were rewarded through crafting," and that the absence of punishment created "a low-stress, forgiving environment that encourages experimentation and exploration." Participants said this ensured engagement without the frustration of potential failure, and that relaxing everyday tasks like farming, crafting, and fishing balanced the emotional weight of the narrative.
requirements: Game mechanics and tasks must remain engaging without overwhelming players
aesthetic and audio elements that convey emotion and comfort
constraints: Derived from one commercially available game and a qualitative player sample; the article presents it as an emergent theory rather than a tested causal design principle
target_learners: players engaging with serious topics such as grief and loss
target_learning_goals: emotional processing of grief and loss
empathy for others' experiences
examples: Spiritfarer downplayed grinding for materials so resource management became enjoyable, and rewarded mistakes through crafting

article_title: Learning teamwork through a computer game: for the sake of performance or collaborative learning?
citation: Elina Riivari, Marke Kivijärvi, Anna-Maija Lämsä. (2021). Learning teamwork through a computer game: for the sake of performance or collaborative learning? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10009-4
title: Novicraft computer-based awareness simulation game for team, leadership, and management training
description: Novicraft is, in the article's words, "a computer-based awareness game, designed particularly for team, leadership, and management training", developed by a multidisciplinary research-based team and informed by learning and motivation theories. Played in real time in teams of three to five on an island-escape scenario, it uses scripts to assign members different resources so that "there is no possibility of free riding to escape from the island as a team". Its five tasks each target different teamwork, collaboration, and leadership skills, and its theoretical basis is Belbin's nine team roles and Kogler Hill's team leadership model.
requirements: Played in teams of three to five with each participant at their own computer, following the developers' recommendation of a maximum of 12 students per session
Trained facilitators who set up the game and act as passive instructors and observers
constraints: Used as a mandatory component of an undergraduate HRM course at a Finnish business school; the game was played in a co-located computer classroom, and the article notes it is no longer available because of technical changes
target_learners: undergraduate university students in a human resource management course
target_learning_goals: teamwork skills
team roles
internal team leadership actions
decision making in teams
examples: In the studied course, teams completed five sequential island-escape tasks, such as negotiating ingredient combinations for burner oil and coordinating fence-building to pass a dog-guarded field

article_title: The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data
citation: Kaitlyn G. Fitzgerald and Elizabeth Tipton. (2022). The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2022.2031366
title: Normative four-criterion framework for visualizing meta-analytic clearinghouse evidence for decision-making
description: The article proposes that visualizations of clearinghouse meta-analytic data should be judged against four normative goals derived from meta-analytic decision theory: they "ought to visually emphasize: 1. Precise studies over imprecise studies, 2. Summary effects over individual effects, 3. The magnitude of the summary effect, and 4. The uncertainty of the summary effect via a range of plausible values." The framework holds that decision-making should rest on the inverse-variance weighted average effect, judged against a user-defined magnitude threshold and communicated with uncertainty that gives intuition about the range of plausible true effects. It motivates the MARC plot's design choices, such as omitting individual-study confidence intervals to discourage vote-counting.
requirements: Because practitioners cannot be expected to know meta-analytic methods, visualizations must intuitively guide them toward normative meta-analytic thinking without requiring training
constraints: The framework focuses on decisions about the average treatment effect, because the current evidence landscape does not yet allow locally contextualized predictive decision-making
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of meta-analytic evidence (effect magnitude, precision, uncertainty) for adoption decisions
examples: The authors used the criteria to critique WWC bar plots, forest plots, and rainforest plots, noting bar plots draw attention to large but imprecise effects and forest plots give imprecise studies undue visual attention
key_sources: Kaitlyn G. Fitzgerald and Elizabeth Tipton. (2022). The Meta-Analytic Rain Cloud Plot: A New Approach to Visualizing Clearinghouse Data. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2022.2031366

article_title: From operating room to leadership room: a systematic review of simulation-based interventions for leadership development in general surgery.
citation: Gulnaz Nadia, Soomro Faiza Hashim, Nazir Izza, Ansar Mehwish, Arshad Rabia. (2026). From operating room to leadership room: a systematic review of simulation-based interventions for leadership development in general surgery. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09486-z
title: NOTSS as the predominant validated framework for assessing surgical leadership and non-technical skills
description: The Non-Technical Skills for Surgeons (NOTSS) framework is a behavioral taxonomy rating leadership, situation awareness, decision-making, and communication/teamwork, used in more than two-thirds of the reviewed studies either directly or as a derived system. The review states that "The predominance of NOTSS in particular underscores its acceptance as a reliable framework for evaluating leadership and decision-making in surgical teams." Frameworks such as NOTSS, NOTECHS, and CRM-based models supported standardized measurement and organized feedback, aiding interrater reliability and reproducibility of non-technical skills training.

Validated behavioral rating instruments aligned to the taxonomy's categories and elements
constraints: Leadership and NTS assessments were frequently subjective and dependent on trained raters, introducing potential interrater variability

Decision-making
Situational awareness
Communication and teamwork
examples: Yule et al. (2006) developed the NOTSS prototype behavioral marker system (4-point scale) via cognitive task analysis with consultant surgeons
Abahuje et al. (2022) integrated NOTSS as one of four domains in a mixed-methods surgical course in Rwanda

article_title: Effectiveness of Analogy Instructional Strategy on Undergraduate Student's Acquisition of Organic Chemistry Concepts in Mutah University, Jordan
citation: Nawaf Ahmad Hasan Samara. (2016). Effectiveness of Analogy Instructional Strategy on Undergraduate Student's Acquisition of Organic Chemistry Concepts in Mutah University, Jordan. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(8). https://www.iiste.org
title: Nomenclature of Organic Compounds Achievement Test (NOCAT)
description: The NOCAT is a 20-item multiple-choice achievement test prepared by the researcher to measure undergraduate acquisition of organic chemistry concepts. It covers ten conceptual areas — "albanes, alkenes, alkynes, aromatic compounds, cycloalkanes, aldehydes, ketones, ethers, organic halogen compounds and carboxylic acids" — and was validated by two chemistry educators and two experienced chemistry faculty members for content validity. Each question was scored 1 point, for a maximum of 20 points.
requirements: Content validity was established by examination from two chemistry educators and two experienced chemistry faculty members.

examples: Used as pre-test and post-test in the quasi-experiment; reliability based on Cronbach's alpha was 0.79.

article_title: Evaluating a Pre-Session Homework Exercise in a Standalone Information Literacy Class
citation: Goetz, J. E., & Barber, C. R. (2015). Evaluating a pre-session homework exercise in a standalone information literacy class. Communications in Information Literacy, 9(2). https://pdxscholar.library.pdx.edu/comminfolit/
title: Nonequivalent control group quasi-experimental design for assessing pre-session library instruction within a one-shot session
description: The article adapts Campbell and Stanley's nonequivalent control group design to standalone library instruction: treatment and control sections are pre-existing course sections rather than individually randomized, and an in-class pretest strengthens evidence that the groups are similar. The librarian retains control of administering and collecting pretests, posttests and surveys within the single session. The authors frame this as a site-specific methodological strategy for evaluating pre-session homework independently of identical in-class instruction.
requirements: A pretest to strengthen evidence that pre-existing groups are not significantly different in the measured area
Identical instruction across treatment and control groups apart from the pre-session homework
constraints: Individual random assignment is impractical; differences between groups due to instructors or location cannot be ruled out
The design is not truly experimental
target_learners: graduate students in standalone information literacy sessions
target_learning_goals: information literacy skills such as database thesaurus searching
examples: Treatment and control groups were formed from course sections whose instructors did or did not volunteer the homework handout, with coordinated lesson plans across library instructors

article_title: Helping Students to Automatize Multiplication Facts: A Pilot Study
citation: Barbara Allen-Lyall. (2018). Helping Students to Automatize Multiplication Facts: A Pilot Study. IEJEE, Volume 10, Issue 4, 391-396. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2018438128
title: Non-linear fact-family exploration with partner matching, flip books, and products-grid activities
description: The intervention organized facts practice as exploratory activities rather than sequential drill: students matched product cards with factor-pair cards in tabular arrangements, tested one another with homemade fact flip books, and inspected “interesting nines products relationships on a 10x10 products grid.” Fact families were addressed in non-linear fashion, with sevens and eights explored before fours and sixes, and only two sequential sevens facts worked on at a time to build confidence before fitting the family together as a complete set 1-12.
requirements: Sessions of 30 minutes, one-week intervals, replicated systematically across classrooms by the researcher
constraints: A week was missed on two occasions at each school for state testing and spring vacation, extending the timeframe to twelve weeks
target_learners: Grade 3 students in diverse suburban elementary schools
target_learning_goals: automaticity with single-digit multiplication facts
examples: Students explored square number products 1-12 first, then worked with just two sequential sevens facts, for example 7x6 and 7x7, before the family was fitted together as a complete set

article_title: Concept Mapping Strategy: An Effective Tool for Improving Students' Academic Achievement in Biology
citation: Sakiyo, J. & Waziri, K. (2015). Concept mapping strategy: An effective tool for improving students' academic achievement in biology. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 1(1), 56-62. www.jeseh.net
title: Novak's meaningful learning theory underlying concept mapping
description: The article grounds concept mapping in Novak's account of meaningful learning: "meaningful (as opposed to rote) human learning occurs when new knowledge is consciously and purposively linked to an existing framework of prior knowledge". The mind is said to organize information hierarchically from higher to lower level skills, while rote learning adds concepts arbitrarily and verbatim, producing a weak structure that degenerates. Concept maps represent this organization with propositions, hierarchical branching, cross-links, and specific examples.
requirements: New knowledge must be consciously and purposively linked to the learner's existing framework of prior knowledge for meaningful learning to occur
constraints: The theory as presented is attributed to Novak (2006, 2010) rather than tested in this study
target_learning_goals: meaningful (non-rote) understanding of biology concepts
examples: The article illustrates hierarchy with a plant cell map whose major concepts include Cell Wall, Protoplasm, Cytoplasm, Nucleus and Vacuole arranged from most general at the top to specific below

article_title: Analyzing the Efficacy of the Testing Effect Using Kahoot™ on Student Performance
citation: Iwamoto, D. H., Hargis, J., Taitano, E. J., & Vuong, K. (2017). Analyzing the efficacy of the testing effect using Kahoot on student performance. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 18(2). https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: Use no-stakes gamified retrieval-practice quizzes as exam preparation rather than lecture-based review alone
description: The article recommends replacing part of lecture-based exam review with low-stakes retrieval practice delivered through a game-like quizzing tool, because the testing effect improves retention relative to passive study and because a fun, engaging format supports performance. Both groups received the same key concepts, but the control group got them "in writing and through a lecture" while the experimental group received them as no-stakes Kahoot quizzes, and the quiz group scored significantly higher.
requirements: Quiz questions must align with the key concepts of the upcoming high-stakes exam without duplicating its wording; students must know the quizzes carry no grade consequences
constraints: Evidence comes from one small (n=49) convenience-sampled pilot study in a single instructor's course; the authors note the significant result may reflect Kahoot specifically or gamification generally, and recommend longer, multi-institution replications
target_learning_goals: improved performance on high-stakes summative examinations
examples: The experimental group spent the last 10 minutes of predetermined classes on seven-question Kahoot quizzes and one 50-minute class period replaying all quizzes, while the control group received a written study guide and a 50-minute lecture review

citation: Wael Alshurman, Ihsani Alsreaa. (2015). The Efficiency of Peer Teaching of Developing Non Verbal Communication to Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.29. https://www.iiste.org

Items were retained with 85% inter-referee agreement and 70% expert agreement. Reliability was high: internal consistency "was (0.9666) for the total scale", and item-total correlations ranged between 0.89-0.95.

constraints: Validated on exploratory samples of 10 children outside the study sample
target_learners: children with autism spectrum disorder aged 8-12
target_learning_goals: measuring non-verbal communication skills
examples: Content validity was checked by a panel of 9 university faculty members in special education; test-retest reliability was established over two weeks

article_title: To Wait in Tier 1 or Intervene Immediately: A Randomized Experiment Examining First Grade Response to Intervention (RTI) in Reading
citation: Al Otaiba, S., Connor, C. M., Folsom, J. S., Wanzek, J., Greulich, L., Schatschneider, C., & Wagner, R. K. (2015). To Wait in Tier 1 or Intervene Immediately: A Randomized Experiment Examining First Grade Response to Intervention (RTI) in Reading. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Do not delay intensive intervention for the weakest first-grade readers; fast-track them immediately
description: Based on their randomized findings, the authors recommend against waiting: "Dynamic RTI protocols, such as the one used in this study, suggest that there is no reason to delay intervention, that any effect of false negatives is negligible, and that, broadly implemented, Dynamic RTI, including a foundation of effective Tier 1 instruction, can improve reading outcomes for all children." This addresses concerns that early screening unreliability would produce false positives, and informs the debate about RTI becoming another wait-to-fail model.
requirements: A foundation of effective Tier 1 instruction
Initial screening with teacher reports and multiple screeners using local norms
constraints: Findings come from one district's first year of RTI implementation; the authors note some districts may use versions of RTI similar to both conditions
target_learners: First-grade students with the weakest reading skills
target_learning_goals: Improving end-of-first-grade reading outcomes for all children
examples: The experiment fast-tracked students scoring below the 40th percentile on all four screeners with teacher-reported severe difficulties directly to Tier 3 at the September screening.

article_title: The Effects of Focused/Unfocused Audio-Appended Reading Tasks on Intermediate Female EFL Learners' Written Accuracy
citation: Alavinia, P., Shafaei, A., & Salimi, A. (2018). The Effects of Focused/Unfocused Audio-Appended Reading Tasks on Intermediate Female EFL Learners' Written Accuracy. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 203-220. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11214a
title: Noticing hypothesis and implicit focus-on-form as the explanatory account for the focused-task advantage
description: The article explains its findings through Schmidt's noticing hypothesis, that "second language acquisition is largely driven by what learners pay attention to and notice in target language input", and through Ellis's implicit focus-on-form instruction. Highlighting target forms in texts, audio emphasis, and teacher intonation and repetition are treated as attention-drawing devices that convert input into intake. The authors conclude learners "who were exposed to focused reading tasks benefited from the implicit FOF strategies used in the present study".
requirements: Instruction must draw learners' attention to target forms while they engage in meaning-focused reading, e.g. via highlighting, audio, intonation changes and repetition
constraints: Account offered as authors' interpretation of a single quasi-experiment with female intermediate learners; no direct measure of noticing was reported
target_learning_goals: written grammatical accuracy in rule-bound and non-rule-bound structures
examples: Focused groups received highlighted texts with audio files, teacher re-reading with intonation changes and repetition of target structures, and end-of-session exercises on those forms

article_title: On the Role of Media Input in the Learning of Formulaic Sequences by EFL Learners
citation: Didem Koban Koç & Serdar Engin Koç. (2017). On the Role of Media Input in the Learning of Formulaic Sequences by EFL Learners. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 34(3), 93–110. https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1275
title: Noticing Hypothesis as the article's explanatory account for media-supported retention of formulaic sequences
description: The article interprets its retention result through Schmidt's (1990) Noticing Hypothesis, which holds that learners cannot acquire a language form unless they notice it in the input, so "the first step in the acquisition of a language is paying attention to forms." The authors state that "The results are also in support of Schmidt’s (1990) Noticing Hypothesis that emphasized the role of attention and awareness in adult second language acquisition," arguing that seeing FSs used in visual contexts helped learners retain them longer. The study's procedure operationalizes noticing by having the instructor draw attention to each FS after clip viewing.
requirements: Instructors must draw learners' attention to the target FSs and provide definitions after exposure
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of one small experimental study, not a tested mechanism in the study itself
target_learning_goals: learning and retention of formulaic sequences
examples: After each clip, the instructor drew the participants' attention to the FS and provided its definition

citation: Admiraal, W., Janssen, T., Huizenga, J., Kranenburg, F., Taconis, R., & Corda, A. (2014). E-assessment of student-teachers’ competence as new teachers. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 13(4). https://www.tojet.net/

citation: Isazadeh, P., Makui, S. M. Z., & Ansarian, L. (2016). Effect of Instructional vs. Authentic Video Materials on Introvert and Extrovert Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.4n.4p.1
title: Do not separate EFL learners into matched classes by introversion and extroversion when showing movies for vocabulary learning
description: The article concludes that forming classes matched on introversion/extroversion is unnecessary when video materials are used for vocabulary learning, because the comparative effect of the two video types showed no significant difference for extroverts and only a modest introvert difference. It states "there is no need to separate language learners into matched classes in terms of introversion and extroversion while showing movies to them". The finding is specific to vocabulary learning with video in an Iranian EFL context.
requirements: Learners' introversion/extroversion would otherwise need to be assessed, e.g. with the Eysenck Personality Inventory, before forming matched classes
constraints: Based on one study of intermediate adult learners at a single language institute; the introvert group did benefit more from authentic video, so style may still matter for material choice within a class

examples: After three weeks of treatment, the authentic-video and instructional-video extrovert groups did not differ significantly, and the authors advise against style-matched classes for movie-based instruction

Dictogloss is presented as a focused task that creates a situation where students notice the gap between their interlanguage output and the target language.
requirements: Learners must consciously notice target forms in the input for acquisition to occur
constraints: The article applies the framework to intermediate/pre-intermediate EFL learners in Iranian high schools

second language form acquisition

description: The article invokes Schmidt's noticing hypothesis to explain why self-correction produced the largest gains: "Second language learners could not begin to acquire a language feature until they had become aware of it in the input". The article uses this account to interpret its quasi-experimental results.

constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive explanation for its findings, not as a directly tested component.

noticing of pronunciation errors

article_title: The Effectiveness of Visual Input Enhancement on the Noticing and L2 Development of the Spanish Past Tense
citation: Loewen, S., & Inceoglu, S. (2016). The effectiveness of visual input enhancement on the noticing and L2 development of the Spanish past tense. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 6(1), 89-110. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2016.6.1.5
title: Schmidt's noticing hypothesis and the distinction between attention and awareness in L2 learning.
description: The article describes Schmidt's (1990) noticing hypothesis, which claims that learners must consciously notice forms in the input for acquisition to take place. It further explains that the term noticing conflates two different constructs: attention, described by Robinson as detection plus rehearsal in working memory and a continuous construct, and awareness, which involves conscious recognition of attended stimuli and can be viewed as a dichotomous construct. The article uses this framework to structure its research questions, with RQ1 addressing attention via eye tracking and RQ2 addressing awareness via self-report.
requirements: Measures of noticing must distinguish between attention and awareness as separate constructs.
constraints: The exact characteristics of noticing, attention and awareness in L2 learning remain controversial.
target_learning_goals: attention to and awareness of L2 grammatical forms in written input
examples: The study operationalized attention as eye-tracking fixation times and awareness as exit questionnaire self-reports coded for level of awareness.

examples: The study compared impulsive, reflective, and control groups on an IELTS reading test and found no significant differences
