citation: Sahin Abdul Samet, Yilmaz Mutlu, Imamoglu Melih, Beser Muhammet Fatih, Karaca Yunus, Pasli Sinan, Gunduz Abdulkadir. (2026). Effectiveness and retention of extremity and junctional tourniquet training among medical interns. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09111-z
title: Novelty-driven deep processing account of differential skill retention
description: The authors propose that the differential retention between junctional and extremity tourniquet skills may be explained by a 'Novelty Effect': "because the junctional tourniquet was perceived as a sophisticated and high-stakes intervention, it triggered 'deep processing' and increased activation in the hippocampus and dopaminergic systems, leading to more resilient neural encoding compared to the 'familiar' extremity tourniquet." They further suggest that junctional application involves more sequential procedural steps that may be more effectively encoded in long-term procedural memory, whereas extremity application relies on automated repetitive motor tasks more susceptible to fading.
requirements: Perceived novelty and clinical salience of the material to trigger deeper cognitive engagement
constraints: A ceiling effect in the six-item junctional checklist may lack the granularity of the ten-item extremity tool, potentially masking subtle performance declines
Proposed as interpretation, not tested directly in this study
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of psychomotor clinical skills

article_title: Comparative validation of a cost-effective in-house 3D-printed LLETZ simulator versus a commercial training model.
citation: Scherer-Quenzer AC, Reinhart K, Diessner J, Altides A, Buechel J, Blau-Schneider B, Sauer ST, Deschler-Baier B, Woeckel A, Kiesel M. (2026). Comparative validation of a cost-effective in-house 3D-printed LLETZ simulator versus a commercial training model. Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00404-026-08413-3
title: For training surgical novices, prioritize simulator designs that maximize visibility and material consistency over maximal realism
description: The article argues that for novice training, a simulator's accessibility matters more than clinical realism: the in-house model's "wider vaginal opening allows for greater speculum expansion, enhancing visualization of the cervix", its agar–agar material gives more consistent excisions, and lower smoke output "creates a more accessible learning environment". The commercial model's narrower canal, meat-based material, and smoke production made it more challenging without benefiting novices.
requirements: Training goal must be novice skill acquisition rather than advanced-trainee realism practice
constraints: The authors note more complex simulators may better simulate clinical reality and could suit advanced trainees, though their resident data did not show the in-house model was too easy
target_learners: medical students without prior procedural experience
target_learning_goals: electrosurgical excision technique
learning progression toward consistent resection quality
examples: The study assigned novices to either simulator and found the in-house group's LEEP scores decreased consistently while the commercial group's scores rose again after attempt three, which the authors attribute to meat-based model variability and smoke-impaired visibility
key_sources: Scherer-Quenzer AC, Reinhart K, Diessner J, Altides A, Buechel J, Blau-Schneider B, Sauer ST, Deschler-Baier B, Woeckel A, Kiesel M. (2026). Comparative validation of a cost-effective in-house 3D-printed LLETZ simulator versus a commercial training model. Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00404-026-08413-3

article_title: A cross-sectional comparison of nursing knowledge attitudes and practices in adverse event management based on simulation training experience.
citation: Shen Yi, Wang Ye, Wu Shiyu, Yang Rumei, He Ming, Ma Qi. (2026). A cross-sectional comparison of nursing knowledge attitudes and practices in adverse event management based on simulation training experience. Scientific Reports 16, 8401. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-39781-0
title: Institutions should implement non-punitive reporting systems and provide ongoing support to mitigate nurses' fears about reporting adverse events
description: Nurses' attitude data showed hesitancy around reporting consequences: 42.75% were neutral about whether reporting an ANE involving a colleague would offend that colleague, and concerns about promotion and commendation were evident. The article states: "To mitigate these concerns, healthcare institutions should prioritize the implementation of non-punitive reporting systems and provide ongoing support and resources to facilitate effective ANE reporting and resolution." This principle frames reporting culture as an organizational responsibility supporting learning from adverse events.
requirements: Organizational commitment to non-punitive reporting policy and resourced support for reporters
constraints: Grounded in this study's self-reported attitude data from five Chinese hospitals with existing CSSC programs; the authors cite patient safety culture literature rather than testing this intervention
target_learning_goals: willingness to report adverse events including minor and peer-involved events; engagement in post-event analysis and improvement
examples: In the attitude items, 42.75% of nurses were neutral about whether reporting a colleague's ANE would offend that colleague

article_title: Medical Students' Perception of Automated Note Feedback After Simulated Encounters.
citation: S. Bansal, M. Yadav, J. Zhou, R. A. Ebert‐Allen, R. M. Klute, W. F. Bond, S. Bhat. (2025). Medical Students' Perception of Automated Note Feedback After Simulated Encounters. The Clinical Teacher 22(6): e70273. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70273
title: NoteBoost automated patient note grading system
description: NoteBoost is an internally developed NLP-based software system that grades patient notes by finding "checklist items in a patient note and checks for phrases and paraphrases that are close matches to a checklist item." It generates individualized reports listing items found and not found in history and physical sections, shares case diagnosis and alternative diagnoses, and presents feedback through a web-based interface with color-coded visual cues.
requirements: Requires accuracy verification checks before deployment
constraints: Does not address writing style
Does not explain likelihood ratios of physical exam findings
Occasional phrase recognition errors and false positives
target_learning_goals: Patient note writing
History and physical documentation
Differential diagnosis generation
examples: Deployed after two standardized patient encounters (headache and back pain) with 20 minutes for information gathering and 10 minutes for note typing
key_sources: S. Bansal, M. Yadav, J. Zhou, R. A. Ebert‐Allen, R. M. Klute, W. F. Bond, S. Bhat. (2025). Medical Students' Perception of Automated Note Feedback After Simulated Encounters. The Clinical Teacher 22(6): e70273. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70273

article_title: Beyond additive genetic effects: Explaining family resemblance in school performance across millions of pairs of Norwegian relatives.
citation: Eftedal, N. H., Eilertsen, E. M., Sunde, H. F., Kleppestø, T. H., Ystrom, E., & Czajkowski, N. O. (2025). Beyond additive genetic effects: Explaining family resemblance in school performance across millions of pairs of Norwegian relatives. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, 122(25). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2419627122
title: Publicly shared correlation dataset and R scripts for modeling family resemblance in school performance
description: The article releases anonymized correlation data covering 82 categories of relatives on eight national standardized tests, plus R scripts for reproducing the Fisherian analyses. The authors state that "By publicly sharing our correlation data through this paper, we enable other researchers to fit and evaluate alternative models of their choosing." The data are deposited in Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/JFW2K), and supplementary files include correlations for all separate tests and grade-level averages.
requirements: Researchers need the released correlation files and R scripts, available through Open Science Framework, to fit and evaluate alternative models.
constraints: The released data are sets of correlations rather than individual-level records, and same-sex twins of unknown zygosity are excluded from model fitting.
target_learners: Norwegian school students in grades 5, 8, and 9
target_learning_goals: Math achievement
Reading comprehension achievement
English reading achievement
examples: The article's SI Appendix includes files with all correlations for separate tests and grade-level averages, plus R scripts for running the analyses.

article_title: "My skills are going to be exposed" - Anxiety, meaning and professional identity during simulation-based learning in medical students: A mixed method study.
citation: Drake Gareth, Skaltsa Niki, Kalia Kritika, Ogbonnaya Chibueze, Padhair Asha, Morrish Samuel, Nambyiah Pratheeban. (2025). “My skills are going to be exposed” – Anxiety, meaning and professional identity during simulation-based learning in medical students: A mixed method study. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0327306
title: Normalise anxiety and build tolerance of the unknown rather than solely imparting medical expertise
description: A design principle for medical education: rather than treating recall under pressure as the hallmark of competence, the article argues that “educational and pastoral interventions that normalise anxiety while supporting students to place emphasis on a capacity to tolerate the unknown” are likely more useful than interventions that solely impart expertise, reframing competence as including asking for help and navigating uncertainty.
requirements: Educators who adopt a non-judgemental, accepting stance and normalise feelings of anxiety in relation to uncertainty
constraints: The article grounds this in student self-report from a single cohort and cautions that inferences beyond the particular participant group studied must be made cautiously
target_learning_goals: professional identity formation
tolerating uncertainty and seeking help in clinical practice
examples: Students reported a favourable experience of the non-judgemental and accepting stance of educators during debriefs.

article_title: Use of an observer tool to enhance learning of anaesthesia resident's non-technical skills during high-fidelity simulation: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Havard C, Jouffroy V, Le Gouez A, Bruyère M, Figueiredo S, Roulleau P, Benhamou D, Margat A, Blanié A. (2025). Use of an observer tool to enhance learning of anaesthesia resident's non-technical skills during high-fidelity simulation: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education 25:97. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06608-3
title: Paper-based non-technical observer tool based on the ANTS framework
description: A paper observation tool filled in progressively by learning observers during each simulated scenario. It was "constructed using items from the Anaesthetists' Non-Technical Skills (ANTS) based on Fletcher et al.", covering work organisation, teamwork, situational awareness and decision-making, with sub-items rated on a four-point Likert scale (poor, insufficient, acceptable, excellent). Residents were told it was for learning only, not evaluation, and it was completed for 93.7% of assigned observations.
requirements: Completed progressively by observers during each scenario; residents informed it reinforces learning rather than evaluation
constraints: The authors state the tool contained abstract concepts for non-expert users and that its construction may not have been appropriate; design questions (paper versus electronic, length, number of items, word choice) remain and prior training in the tool could have improved its impact
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills: task management, teamwork, situation awareness, decision-making
examples: In the trial, observers in the OT+ group filled the tool during observation of four crisis scenarios (malignant hyperthermia, local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, haemorrhagic shock, post-anaesthesia respiratory arrest) before actively performing a scenario themselves.
key_sources: Havard C, Jouffroy V, Le Gouez A, Bruyère M, Figueiredo S, Roulleau P, Benhamou D, Margat A, Blanié A. (2025). Use of an observer tool to enhance learning of anaesthesia resident's non-technical skills during high-fidelity simulation: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education 25:97. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06608-3

article_title: Long-term effect of pharmacological treatment on academic achievement of Norwegian children diagnosed with ADHD: a target trial emulation.
citation: Varnet Pérez, Tomás; Øvergaard, Kristin Romvig; Frigessi, Arnoldo; Biele, Guido. (2025). Long-term effect of pharmacological treatment on academic achievement of Norwegian children diagnosed with ADHD: a target trial emulation. International Journal of Epidemiology. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyaf010
title: Linked Norwegian registry dataset for the ADHD target trial emulation (NorPD, NPR, KUHR, SSB, MBRN)
description: The study linked person-, family-, and school-level variables from five Norwegian registries: the Norwegian Prescription Database, the Norwegian Patient Registry, the Database for Control and Payment of Health Reimbursement, Statistics Norway, and the Medical Birth Registry of Norway. The analytic sample comprised 8458 children with a complete washout (11,835 in the no-washout sensitivity sample), drawn from about 550 thousand children born 2000–2007. The study population was restricted to Norwegian-born children, limiting generalizability.
requirements: Registry linkage permissions; sensitive data could not be shared, and code for data linkage and preparation is available only upon request
constraints: Lack of prescription data on intended daily dose, treatment duration, and prescription purpose required an algorithm to estimate dosages and duration, introducing additional uncertainty
target_learners: Norwegian-born children diagnosed with ADHD born 2000–2007
target_learning_goals: grade eight national test scores in English, numeracy, and reading
examples: Baseline covariates included grade five national test scores, parental civil status and education, birth variables, and counts of registered health visits prior to time-zero
key_sources: Varnet Pérez, Tomás; Øvergaard, Kristin Romvig; Frigessi, Arnoldo; Biele, Guido. (2025). Long-term effect of pharmacological treatment on academic achievement of Norwegian children diagnosed with ADHD: a target trial emulation. article_title: Deep Learning Analysis of Surgical Video Recordings to Assess Nontechnical Skills.
citation: Harari Rayan Ebnali PhD, Dias Roger D. MD PhD, Kennedy-Metz Lauren R. PhD, Varni Giovanna PhD, Gombolay Matthew PhD, Yule Steven PhD, Salas Eduardo PhD, Zenati Marco A. MD. (2024). Deep Learning Analysis of Surgical Video Recordings to Assess Nontechnical Skills. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.22520
title: NOTSS framework applied at the surgical team level with four nontechnical skill categories
description: The Non-Technical Skills for Surgeons (NOTSS) behavioral rating system, here applied to the collective performance of the whole surgical team rather than an individual surgeon. The article states raters "assessed overall teams’ nontechnical skills along 12 items (behavioral elements) grouped in the following 4 categories: situational awareness, decision-making, communication and teamwork, and leadership." Each item uses a 4-point Likert scale from poor to good performance, and scores are averaged across raters per case. The framework serves as the ground-truth criterion against which the automated motion features were validated.
requirements: Trained raters who have undergone standardized NOTSS training; retrospective video review sessions for rating; scores averaged across raters.
constraints: The NOTSS scale operates on a constricted 1-to-4 range, which the authors say may have compounded rating inconsistencies; low 3-rater interrater reliability was observed.
target_learners: surgical teams in the operating room, including attending surgeons, anesthesiologists, perfusionists, and nurses
target_learning_goals: assessing and developing team nontechnical skills: situational awareness, decision-making, communication and teamwork, and leadership
examples: Mean NOTSS category scores across the 30 cases were 3.3 for situational awareness, 3.2 for decision-making, 3.3 for communication and teamwork, and 3.2 for leadership.
